title: Chapter 20: Certified Copy
content: Mars Okonjo is in the yard at 6:15 in the morning with her headlights on the fence and a folded sheet of paper in her fist, and she does not get out of the car.
"Sixty-one," she says through the window.
Wren stands in the cold with her coat over her arm and reads the sheet upside down. It is a docket printout. Four columns. Names, numbers, dates, and a status column that says OPEN sixty-one times.
"Sixty-one what."

"Matters on your docket. As of last night." Mars hands it out the window. "There is a rule. Local rule twelve, subsection b. If one petitioner carries more than fifty unresolved matters past forty-five days, the court has to set a hearing. It does not have a choice. Nobody has to agree to it. The judge does not have to like you."
Wren counts down the column with her thumb and stops at thirty.
"There are not sixty-one names here."

"There are forty-one names and twenty other things." Mars gets out of the car, because Mars cannot deliver news sitting down. "Twenty of your dead men had a wife or a child on the tax roll. So a deputy clerk opened an estate file for each one, to have somewhere to put the money."
"An estate."

"A dead man cannot own a truck. So the county opened a file saying the truck is nobody's until somebody proves he is dead." Mars puts her hands in her pockets. "They can open an estate for a man they will not certify the death of. That is not a contradiction to them. That is two departments."
Wren reads the sheet again and does the arithmetic on the hood of the car with her finger in the dew.
Forty-one and twenty is sixty-one. One short. She needs one more to cross the line, and she has one more, sitting in a truck outside the diner with a cup of coffee he is not drinking.
"Sixty-two by nine o'clock," she says.
Mars looks at her for a second. Then she says, "Get in. I will buy you a breakfast you will not eat."
At 8:31 Wren rings the bell at the Annex window with the forty-second Form 9 in her hand.

Hollis Drane has stopped pretending about the drawer. He has stopped pretending about a lot of things since October. He takes the form, checks the boxes, and does not ask her what CARRIER means, because he already knows and it has been bothering him for a month.
"Section six," he says.
"Drowned."
"State the basis."
"Nine souls on the cable, 7:20 p.m., 22 October. He went in after a child and did not come up." She puts the second page down. "Two witnesses. The mother and the man who held the stern."
Hollis reads it. His mouth works. "I knew this boy when he was eleven and he used to sit on the steps outside this office and wait for his brother."
"Then stamp it."
He stamps it. The sound is the same small wet sound as all the others, and Wren has begun to think of it as the only sound the county makes.
"Receipt."
"Seven seven one six one."

Bram puts nine dollars on the counter before she can get to the coffee can. Three ones and a five and a quarter. Hollis counts it twice, which is the rule, and writes the receipt by hand with the carbon paper folded wrong, and does not say anything about the quarter.

Behind them the queue has gone quiet the way a queue does when everybody has decided to listen. A woman in a nurse's coat with a dog license in her hand. Two men who came for a fence permit. The photographer from the county paper, who has not taken a picture and is not going to, because he has learned that the pictures that matter happen at the edges of the room.
Wren does not turn around. She has learned that too.
Then Hollis looks at the docket printout on the counter, which Wren did not mean to put there.
"Sixty-two," he says.
"Sixty-two."
"That is over fifty."
"It is."
He looks at the clock. Then he takes his glasses off and cleans them on the hem of his cardigan, which is the most violent thing Wren has ever seen him do.
"They will have to set it," he says. "I have been at this window nineteen years and nobody has ever made them set one."
At 11:20 a deputy clerk finds her in the hallway outside the records room and hands her a single sheet with a raised seal on it, still warm from the machine.
NOTICE OF HEARING. IN THE MATTER OF FORTY-TWO CERTIFICATES OF LOSS, DISTRICT 4.
Docket 26-CV-0631. Saturday, 14 November 2026, 9:00 a.m., Courtroom 2, County Courthouse, 210 Market Street.
Set upon the court's own motion.
Wren reads that last line four times. Nobody signed off on it. Nobody agreed. The county did it the way a pump does it, because the water came up past a mark.
Eleven days.
Mars comes out of the records room with her lanyard swinging and reads the sheet over her shoulder.
"What happens in there," Wren says.
"One hour. The judge reads the docket off the sheet and asks what you are asking for."
"One word."

"Then he asks them why they will not write it." Mars folds her arms. "They will send a lawyer from Columbus who has never seen this river. He will say cause of death is a medical determination. He will say the office lacks jurisdiction over a federal release. He will say the file is under review, which takes forty seconds to say and means nothing."
"And then."

"And then the judge decides, and a stenographer writes it down, and for the first time in this county the deciding gets written by somebody who is paid to write it." Mars looks at her. "That is all a hearing is. A room where the record has to be made out loud."
"Now the copies," Mars says.
"What copies."

"Certified copies of everything you filed. All forty-two. The form, the attachment, the receipt." Mars taps the notice. "At a hearing the judge will not look at a photocopy. He will look at a page with a seal on it and a signature under the seal and a date. That is the only version of the truth they recognize. Everything else is paper."
"I have the yellow receipts."
"You have carbon paper. Carbon paper is a rumor." Mars takes her by the elbow, which she does only when she is being kind. "Come on. Window three."
Window three is the county clerk's office, and window three is a woman named Delia who has been stamping things for twenty-six years and has the forearms to prove it.
"Certified copies," Wren says. "Forty-two documents."
Delia does not look up. "One dollar a page. Three dollars a seal."
Wren sets the coffee can on the counter. It is the same can, and it is lighter than it was in October, and there is a folded twenty in the bottom that Ruthie put there without saying so.

The rest is fares. Two dollars a head, four or five people at a time, counted onto the truck seat at the landing in the dark, from people who put the bills down and stepped back and did not want to be thanked. She has never once had to ask for it. That is the part she will not say out loud in a courtroom, because it sounds like boasting and it is not.
Delia feeds the pages into the machine and works an adding machine with one finger, and the tape comes out and she tears it and reads it.
"Two hundred and ninety-six dollars."
Wren counts. Fives, ones, a roll of quarters from the landing jar. It takes eleven minutes. Delia counts it twice the way Hollis does, and then she starts the seals.
The machine is old. It comes down on each document with a thud she can feel in the counter, and Delia signs each certificate page in blue ink, and the stack grows.
Bram leans on the rail and watches the page count climb on the machine's little window and says, at one hundred and seventy, "That is a lot of paper for one word."
"That is the point," Wren says. "There is no other way to make one word weigh anything."
When the last seal lands, Delia squares the stack and puts a rubber band around it and pushes it across.
Bram puts his hand flat on top of it before Wren can take it.
"One of those is mine," he says. "Which one is his."
"Forty-two."
"How much."
"Six pages. Nine dollars."

Bram takes a ten out of his wallet, and Delia makes change out of her own purse, and he puts the dollar back in his pocket and keeps the receipt, and folds it into his shirt pocket where men keep things they intend to keep.
Wren opens the stack at the forty-first document and reads the certificate page. It is a form with the seal pressed into the paper so hard the page has gone thin.
I CERTIFY that the attached is a true and correct copy of a document on file in this office.
Underneath, the attached document says, in the box marked STATUS, one word. PENDING.
She reads it twice.
"So they certified that nothing is certified."
"Yes," Mars says.
"That is the whole thing. That is the whole trick of this town."

"That is what a record is." Mars takes the page and turns it in the light so the seal catches. "It is not the truth. It is a receipt for the truth. You have been asking them for the truth for fifty days. Ask them for the receipt."
Wren puts the certificate down and asks Delia for one more thing, and Delia has to go into the back to find it, and comes out with a single wide page from the index binder.
PENDING CERTIFICATES OF LOSS, DISTRICT 4. Forty-two lines. Name, date of loss, mile, cause, status.

The cause column is blank on all forty-two. Every status says PENDING. Her grandfather's line is the forty-first, and Ade Kessler's is the forty-second, filed that morning at 8:31, and his line is the newest thing on the page and looks exactly like all the others.
"Certify this."
Delia looks at her over the half glasses. "It is a public index. You can have a copy for a dollar."
"I want it certified."
"It says nothing."
"It says forty-two," Wren says. "Certify that."
Delia certifies it. Thud. Blue ink. Three dollars and a dollar.

They are on the steps at ten past two with a stack of paper the size of a suitcase and the cold coming up off the pavement, and Bram has the truck running at the curb because he does not believe in idling in the cold but he does believe in warmth for other people.
Wren goes back inside because there is one box left on the form Delia gave her.
PETITIONER. COUNSEL OF RECORD.

She has filled in everything else. Name, address, 9 Ferry Lane, East Bank. Telephone, which is the diner's number, because the ferry house has not had a phone since 2018. Capacity, where she wrote FERRYMAN and Delia did not blink.
Delia looks at the empty box.
"Who is representing you," she says.
Wren caps the pen.
"My grandfather," she says.
highlight: Sixty-one open matters force a docket, and Wren pays for certified copies that still say pending.
